acceptedAnswer.text: Compression reduces bytes on disk and in memory, which lowers storage costs, cuts I/O, and speeds up analytical queries—even when decompression uses some CPU.

mainEntity.name: What kinds of database compression exist?

acceptedAnswer.text: Two broad approaches are common: row-based (pages of mixed row data compressed as blocks) and column-based (each column stored and encoded separately).
By storing similar values together, column stores can apply encodings like dictionary, run-length, bit-packing, and delta; general codecs such as LZ4 or ZSTD can be layered on top.
Database compression is typically lossless—the original values are recovered exactly. Some systems also support lossy strategies like sampling or reduced precision when exactness isn’t required.

mainEntity.name: What are best practices to maximize compression?

acceptedAnswer.text: Choose tighter data types, model low-cardinality strings as enums, avoid unnecessary precision, match codecs to data patterns (e.g., delta for time), and measure results per column.

mainEntity.name: What trade-offs exist between CPU and I/O?

acceptedAnswer.text: Decompression costs CPU, but in analytical workloads the I/O saved by reading fewer bytes usually outweighs the CPU overhead, resulting in faster queries overall.

mainEntity.name: Which databases achieve the best compression?

acceptedAnswer.text: Benchmarks show columnar systems can be far smaller on disk than row-based ones for the same dataset; ClickHouse, for example, stores some benchmark datasets over 10× smaller than PostgreSQL.

mainEntity.name: Why do columnar databases often query faster?

acceptedAnswer.text: They scan less data and exploit cache locality; compressed column chunks reduce I/O and allow engines to apply vectorized operations efficiently.

mainEntity.name: When should I avoid storing unnecessary precision?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your use case doesn’t need microsecond timestamps or 64-bit floats, truncating precision shrinks data and can improve compression and performance without harming results.

mainEntity.name: What encodings help most with time-series data?

acceptedAnswer.text: Delta and double-delta encodings are effective for monotonic sequences like timestamps; run-length can help when values repeat, and bit-packing compresses bounded integer ranges.
